1.0.0.en: There was an old enmity between the children of Israel and the people of Moab, who lived beside them, ever since Saul smote them (1 Sam 14:47). Then they became servants to David (2 Sam 8:2, 12; 1 Chr 18:2), and they were also subject to Solomon, and subject to Israel after the division, paying tribute to the children of Israel (2 Kgs 3:4). So when Ahab king of Israel died, Moab seized the opportunity and rebelled against Israel in order to be rid of the tribute.

1.1.1.en: Upper chamber: an upper room in his palace.

1.1.2.en: Ekron: one of the five great cities of the Philistines, and the farthest of them to the north. Today it is "Aqir," a village about twenty km south of Jaffa.

1.1.3.en: Baalzebub: its meaning is the god of flies, and he was the god worshipped in the city of Ekron. The Jews called him Beelzebub, that is, the god of filth (refuse), to despise his standing. Baalzebub was the most important of the Philistine gods; for this reason the Jews called him the prince of the demons when they spoke with Christ (Mt 12:24). King Ahaziah fell through a window in an upper chamber of his palace and was severely injured. Instead of seeking healing from God, he turned to the pagan gods, and sent messengers to the priests of the god Beelzebub, the god of Ekron, to ask them by means of their god whether he would recover or not.

1.1.4.en: Two great troubles befell Ahaziah, the rebellion of Moab against him and his fall from the lattice, and neither drew him to examine himself, repent and pray. Do you examine yourself when trials befall you, and uncover your sins before God so that He may forgive you and you may change your life and receive His mercies? Or do you make light of it and persist in the snare? Behold, God has given us the opportunity of this life so that we may repent in it; do not waste it, and respond to His calls to you through the events that pass over you.

1.2.0.en: The Tishbite: that is, from the town of Tishbe, which lies in the tribe of Naphtali in the north of the land of the Jews. There is also an opinion that it was a town in Gilead, which lies east of the Jordan.

1.2.1.en: God was angry at Ahaziah's conduct and sent His angel to Elijah the prophet to meet the messengers of Ahaziah who were going to Ekron, and he rebuked them with the word of God, denouncing how they could go to a pagan god, as if there were no God among the children of Israel, though they knew the true God. We note that Elijah knew what had happened from the angel, and this was to show the king's messengers that Elijah's words were from God, because no one knew about this mission except the king and his messengers. The angel asked Elijah to go up because the city of Samaria was built on a hill, so he met the messengers as soon as they came down from the city, and told them God's judgment, and they quickly returned to the king.

1.3.0.en: Before Elijah left them, he told them God's judgment so that they might report it to the king, namely that he would not rise from his bed but would die.

1.4.0.en: The king's messengers did not complete their journey to the priests of Baalzebub, but returned at once to the king, who met them with the question why they had not completed the errand he had given them, since they had come back so quickly.

1.5.0.en: His messengers answered him that a man whom they did not know had met them on the way and commanded them to return to the king who had sent them, and tell him God's judgment on the king, that he would not recover but would die.

1.6.0.en: The king asked them to describe to him the appearance of the man who had met them and spoken these words to them.

1.7.0.en: His messengers told him that he was a hairy man with a girdle of leather about his loins. The king knew at once that he was Elijah the Tishbite. Naturally Ahaziah knew Elijah, because he had seen him when Ahaziah was a youth with his father King Ahab, and had heard much about the power of God that was with him, in addition to his mother Jezebel's distress over him. So he hated him, because Ahaziah was wicked and far from God.

1.8.0.en: The king commissioned a captain of a company of fifty soldiers to seize Elijah. Elijah was sitting on the top of a hill, and the captain called to him from below the hill by the title they were accustomed to address him with, "man of God," informing him of the king's command that he must come down to meet the king. The king did not intend to summon Elijah to receive his blessing, but sent fifty soldiers with their captain to seize him, in anger at the word he had spoken that he would die. Ahaziah sent fifty men because he knew the power of God that was in Elijah, but he did not realize that no number of men can stand before the power of God.

1.8.1.en: The captain called him "man of God" not out of faith in this title, nor with sufficient respect, but because the captain thought he had authority from the king to seize Elijah and that he was under the protection of the pagan gods whom he worshipped like the king, and who in his eyes were stronger than Elijah's God. It is strange that King Ahaziah rejected God's judgment of his death and did not try to repent, though he had been ready to accept a sentence of death by the authority of Baalzebub, for he had sent to ask him whether he would recover or die.

1.8.2.en: Do not resort to sorcerers and demons to know your future or to solve your problems, lest you fall under God's wrath and deserve death and eternal torment. If you are in need, or have fallen into any trial, seek God and be insistent with Him, and do not resort to anyone else, and He will rescue you from all your troubles by His fatherhood and tenderness.

1.9.0.en: Elijah answered the captain of fifty, saying: If I am indeed a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and consume you and your fifty. Indeed fire came down from heaven and consumed the whole company. Elijah said this by a revelation from God, for we see in (v. 15) that the angel told him to go down to the king. So Elijah was not avenging himself for the attempt to seize him; rather it was God who wished to show the weakness of the pagan gods, such as Baalzebub, on whom they relied, and He dealt with the king and the people in the way they understand, that is, with severity, that perhaps they might believe in Him and repent. This is, of course, different from the disciples' request that Christ send fire from heaven, for that contained vengeance and rage, and therefore Christ refused their request (Lk 9:51-56).

1.10.0.en: When Ahaziah learned of the death of the fifty and their captain, he did not examine himself and seek God, but in hardness of heart sent another fifty with their captain with strict orders to seize Elijah. The captain said to him, Make haste and come down to meet the king. Then, as the previous time, Elijah commanded that fire come down from heaven and consume them, so that the king and all the people might know that God is stronger than all the pagan gods, and might respect His man Elijah and the word of God that was on his lips.

1.10.1.en: Here God's longsuffering toward Ahaziah appears, and at the same time Ahaziah's hardness of heart and his refusal to repent.

1.10.2.en: Do not be stubborn against the voice of God, but return to Him in repentance, and He will have mercy on you and forgive your sins. For who are you, that you defy God and provoke Him by your insistence on committing sin and by not benefiting from the events around you and the teachings of the Church, which calls you to repent?

1.11.0.en: In hardness of heart Ahaziah refused to believe in the power of God and had no pity on his soldiers, so he again sent a third fifty, with their captain at their head. But this captain was different from his two predecessors; he was a devout man who feared God and worshipped Him. He did not call to Elijah as the former ones had done, but went up himself to the top of the hill, where Elijah was sitting, bowed down before him, and entreated him to spare his life and the lives of the fifty with him, asking him not to punish them with fire coming down from heaven, as had happened to the two previous missions.

1.12.0.en: Elijah moved only under the guidance of the Lord, so the angel of the Lord reassured him and told him to respond to the request of the captain of fifty and go down with him from the hill. He did so, and went with the captain to the king.

1.13.0.en: Elijah repeated before the king the same message as before, which he had sent to him by his messengers when the king resorted to Baalzebub. Here Elijah's courage and obedience to God appear, for he was ready to endure any hardship, even death, and he proclaimed the word of God with power, that perhaps the king might repent in the last moments of his life; but sadly he did not repent.

1.14.s.en: (3) The death of Ahaziah and the reign of Jehoram

1.14.0.en: The word of the Lord, which He had spoken by the mouth of Elijah, was fulfilled, for King Ahaziah died. His brother Jehoram, the second son of Ahab and Jezebel, ascended the throne of Israel after him, because Ahaziah had no sons. This was in the second year of Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat over the kingdom of Judah. It is noted that Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat reigned with his father in the seventeenth year of his father's reign over Judah, and about two years after Jehoram's reign with his father Jehoshaphat, Joram son of Ahab reigned over Israel in place of his brother Ahaziah who had died.

1.15.0.en: There are historical records of all the acts of Ahaziah and what he did during his reign, written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel. It is a book that existed in the days of those kings and is not among the books of the Holy Bible, and it is different from the First and Second Chronicles.

1.15.1.en: The inevitable result of persisting in evil is destruction. This is what happened to Ahaziah after he made light of God's longsuffering. So remember the judgment, that you may be alert to your sins and hasten to repentance. Remember the judgment at the end of each day with the prayer of the Sleep hour, and when you wake and God gives you a new day, remember the Resurrection of Christ, that you may rise with Him and pray the prayer of the Prime hour from the Agpeya. These prayers help you to repent at the end of each day and to begin with hope at the start of each day.

1.15.2.en: The ascension of Elijah and Elisha succeeding him in prophecy. If the previous chapter tells us of the end of a wicked king, Ahaziah, with his sickness and death, since God's wrath came upon him, in this chapter we find the end of a great prophet, Elijah, who is taken up to heaven in his body, to live in a position of great standing and greatness with God.

2.0.s.en: (1) The taking up of Elijah to heaven in the whirlwind

2.0.0.en: Gilgal: a city lying east of Jericho, four miles away, and north of Bethel, 13 km away, and it lies in the allotment of Ephraim. It is different from the Gilgal where Joshua camped when he entered the land of Canaan. When the Lord decided to take Elijah to heaven in the whirlwind, Elijah and his disciple Elisha were at Gilgal and about to leave it.

2.1.0.en: Bethel: it lies twelve miles from Jerusalem.

2.1.1.en: Elijah wished to be alone on this journey, so he made Elisha understand that he had been sent by the Lord to Bethel and asked him to stay at Gilgal. But Elisha refused and swore not to leave his master. This shows how firmly Elisha held to being a disciple at the hands of Elijah, to receive his blessing and learn from him, especially as God had informed him that the end of Elijah's life was near, as we shall understand from the following verses.

2.1.2.en: We note that Elijah traveled between the towns to visit the sons of the prophets who were in them, to bless them and bid them farewell, since he knew that his departure from this world was near. He told Elisha to stay at Gilgal, perhaps because he wanted solitude with God at the end of his life, or to test how firmly Elisha held to discipleship at his hands. It may also be that the reason was Elijah's attempt to hide his ascent to heaven as a kind of humility.

2.2.0.en: The sons of the prophets: they are the students in the school of the prophets, which Elijah supervised and in which he taught them the spiritual life.

2.2.1.en: When they reached Bethel, the sons of the prophets who lived there came out to meet Elisha and asked him whether he knew that the Lord would take away his master Elijah that day. He answered them that he knew it; let them keep silent, because the matter was grievous to him.

2.3.0.en: Jericho: Jericho is a city lying eight kilometers west of the Jordan River and twenty-seven kilometers northeast of Jerusalem, and about twelve kilometers from Bethel. Again Elijah asked Elisha to stay at Bethel, because the Lord had sent him on a mission to Jericho. Elisha refused, as he had done the previous time, and accompanied his master to Jericho. Here Elijah continues his visiting of the schools of the prophets to reassure them, bid them farewell and encourage them. Elisha likewise continues to hold to his master, to be his disciple until the last moment of his life, and in this he surpasses the disciples of Christ, who slept in the garden of Gethsemane, though Christ had told them that His departure from this world was near.

2.3.1.en: It is also noted how much care Elijah took in visiting and tending his sons the prophets, for he walked long distances between one town and another, a distance estimated at several miles; and likewise Elisha's striving to cling to his master, for he walked with him these long distances, which are thirteen kilometers from Gilgal to Bethel, then twelve kilometers from Bethel to Jericho, then eight kilometers from Jericho to the Jordan River. These distances took long hours, about nine hours or more, and this shows the seriousness and care of these two great prophets.

2.3.2.en: Do not be slack in your prayers and prostrations, for your striving is very precious to God. Respond to His love, for He made light of sufferings for your sake on the Cross. Do not be slack in visiting His children and seeking every person who is far away, as Christ walked for long hours for the sake of the Samaritan woman. He awaits your love, so do not delay.

2.4.0.en: At Jericho the same thing happened again as with the prophets of Bethel (v. 3), and Elisha gave them the same reply.

2.5.0.en: For the third time Elijah told his disciple that the Lord had sent him to the Jordan, and this time also Elisha refused to stay and went on with his master toward the Jordan.

2.6.0.en: The sons of the prophets learned of the coming of Elijah and Elisha, so they came to them, where they stood on the bank of the river, and stood opposite them, that is, at a distance from them, on the same side of the river, that is, the western bank. It is noted that the fifty prophets were from the school of the prophets at Jericho, and this shows the great number of the prophets; for if this number is only some of the prophets of this school, how great must be the number of the prophets in all the schools! This also shows how much Elijah cared about discipling a generation of prophets after him, and also how great God's blessing was in giving prophecy to a large number, and their care to be disciples at the hands of Elijah, all this in the midst of a wicked generation that worshipped idols and was led by wicked kings such as Ahab.

2.7.0.en: Elijah took his mantle, wrapped it together, and struck the water with it, and it divided into two parts, which enabled Elijah and Elisha to cross over on the dry bed of the river to the opposite bank. Here the grace of God appears, which dried the bed of the river so that they might cross it easily.

2.7.1.en: Here a great miracle appears, repeated for the third time, after the dividing of the Red Sea by Moses and the dividing of the Jordan by Joshua, and this was done for the following reasons:

2.7.2.en: 1- So that Elijah's ascent to heaven might take place quietly, and none might see it except Elisha his disciple, who was of a high spiritual level, for only the spiritual can bear these divine sights.

2.7.3.en: 2- The dividing of the river proclaims Elijah's power before the prophets and all the people, that they may hold fast to his teachings and reject the worship of idols.

2.7.4.en: 3- Elisha's passing with Elijah proclaims his standing before the prophets, which would grow more firm, as will appear in the following verses, so that they would submit to him as their leader after Elijah.

2.7.5.en: 4- Elijah's crossing the Jordan with the waters standing on both sides signifies that death is nothing but a departure, as we remember in the Litany of the Departed, because Elijah afterward went up to heaven, and this is a declaration that there is no death for those who believe in God.

2.7.6.en: 5- The crossing of Elijah and Elisha in the Jordan reminded the prophets and the people of the crossing of the Red Sea and of the Jordan before, and all this signifies the sacrament of Baptism, which brings us across from slavery, the worship of idols and evil to the new life with God.

2.8.0.en: When they had crossed over, Elijah said to Elisha: Ask what I shall do for thee, before I be taken away from thee. Elisha asked that a double portion of the spiritual power Elijah had might rest upon him. The inheritance of a double portion is the share of the firstborn when the inheritance is divided, so Elisha asked to be counted as Elijah's firstborn son, because Elijah had chosen him to be a prophet after him (1 Kgs 19:19). Elisha felt his great need and asked for a power to support him in his great prophetic work and his leading of the people of God.

2.8.1.en: This does not mean that Elisha would become greater in spiritual stature than Elijah, but that he would receive a doubled power in working miracles, and this indeed happened, as we shall see in the following chapters.

2.8.2.en: Although Elijah was detached and poor, he possessed everything through his relationship with God, so he said to his disciple, What shall I give you by my prayer? And he gave him more than any gift a rich man gives to others.

2.8.3.en: You possess the greatest power in the world, which is prayer, to satisfy your soul and fill the needs of those around you. So trust in the power of God that is in you and lift up your heart in prayer, and do not look at your weakness, or your poverty, or the multitude of your sins, for repentance restores to you your sonship to God, and you ask of your heavenly Father all that you wish, and you will be answered.

2.9.0.en: Elijah made clear to Elisha that his request was great and difficult, but God, who is able to do all things, would give it to him, because he had not asked for glory or wealth but for the power of God, which would help him in his ministry. He promised him the fulfillment of this request as soon as he saw Elijah's departure from the world, but before seeing it he would receive nothing, for this power is tied to his taking over the leadership of the ministry. His saying "if thou see me" means that spiritual sights are seen only by those to whom God grants it. Gehazi, Elisha's servant, did not see the heavenly hosts that supported his master Elisha until Elisha prayed for him, and his eyes were opened and he saw (ch. 6:17). So if Elisha saw the sight of Elijah ascending, this meant God's seal that Elisha's choice as spiritual leader of the people was confirmed, and He allowed him to see this spiritual sight, which is Elijah's ascent, and consequently to receive at the same time the power to begin his ministry.

2.9.1.en: The divine graces are abundant, and the Lord is ready to give them to those of His children who ask for them, but we must ask for them with persistence, in continual prayer, relying on the promise of the Lord Christ who said: "Seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you" (Mt 7:7), especially if you feel the greatness of the responsibility facing you and your need for God's support.

2.10.0.en: After Elisha crossed the Jordan with his master Elijah, they walked on together on the eastern bank of the river, with Elisha trying to ask his master questions and benefit from him in the last moments of his life. And as they went on, a chariot of fire, drawn by horses of fire, came toward them from heaven. This chariot and its horses are angels, who appeared in this fiery form, as their appearance was repeated to Elisha in (2 Kgs 6:17). Elisha was afraid and drew back to one side, and the chariot parted him from his master Elijah, to proclaim that Elijah was of a high spiritual standing and would be joined to the heavenly ones. Then Elijah mounted this fiery chariot. At that moment Elisha saw a whirlwind carry this chariot and rise with it to heaven, in a great and awesome sight, and Elisha's eyes remained fixed on his master and his fiery chariot until he disappeared from view.

2.10.1.en: Elijah's ascent to heaven confirms that proclaiming the truth is a great virtue, over which heaven rejoices. Therefore Elijah was lifted up because of this virtue, to be with the heavenly ones, and to encourage every person to proclaim the truth whatever great cost it may bring him, even if it costs his life.

2.10.2.en: Perhaps Elijah's ascent in a chariot of fire accords with his fiery life, in his sense of God's presence with him and His power in proclaiming the truth.

2.10.3.en: Elijah's ascent to heaven is a type of Christ's Resurrection and His Ascension into the heavens, to prepare a place for us and to bring us up into the Kingdom after the end of our life on earth.

2.11.0.en: While Elisha was seeing the chariot rise with his master Elijah to heaven and almost disappear from his sight, he was crying out to his master with a loud voice and saying to him "My father," for he was bound to him as to a father and had been a disciple at his hands for long years, nearly sixteen years, in which he saw in his master a strong spiritual leader who led the children of Israel and called them to life with God. Therefore he called him the chariot of Israel and the horsemen thereof, for this chariot which announced the end of Elijah's life on earth is a declaration of his ministry, in which he led the people like one riding in a chariot, with the multitudes of the people following him in the way of God.

2.11.1.en: Elisha was in very great pain at his master's parting from him, and he expressed his deep grief by rending his clothes, which is an ancient Eastern custom practiced by many peoples and still continues today in Upper Egypt.

2.11.2.en: The rending of the clothes also meant his sense of the greatness of the responsibility that had come to him in leading this great people, most of whom were sunk in the worship of idols.

2.11.3.en: Let your eyes be fixed on heaven and on the saints, your fathers who intercede for you, so that you become a disciple of their lives and enjoy their friendship, and your life is lifted up toward heaven and you prepare for the Kingdom.

2.12.0.en: When Elijah went up in the chariot of fire, his mantle fell from him to the ground, and this was of course by God's arrangement so that Elisha might take it, not only as a blessing from his master but because this mantle holds a memory in Elisha's heart that he can never forget, for sixteen years before, Elijah had cast it upon him when he was plowing in his father's fields and called him to ministry, and he continued as a disciple, close beside his master, all that time. Now he begins to practice the ministry to which God had called him, so he took hold of the mantle, that is, of God's calling. And by God's power he is able to begin, and not by himself. This mantle also, only a few hours before, had divided the Jordan River, so that he and Elijah crossed on the dry ground of the river. So this mantle represents the power of God that supports him, like the rod of Moses with which he worked miracles. And when Elisha took hold of Elijah's mantle he stood before the Jordan River to work his first miracle.

2.13.0.en: Elisha wanted to cross the Jordan River to reach the prophets standing on the other bank, that is, the western bank of the Jordan. As he held Elijah's mantle he believed in the power of this mantle, so he struck the water of the river with it so that it would divide and he could cross, as had happened before with Elijah, but nothing happened. He felt that the power is not in the mantle but in God who works through it, so he cried out to God asking His help; and as He had worked with Elijah, he needed Him to work with him now. Therefore he said, Where is the Lord God of Elijah? Then his heart was filled with stronger faith and he did not doubt, but took up the mantle and struck the river with it, and it divided into two parts, so that Elisha crossed between them. Thus it appeared to the prophets, and consequently to all the people, that as Elijah had divided the river, so Elisha also divided it, that is, that the power of God that had been working in Elijah is the same that works in Elisha.

2.13.1.en: Be steadfast in your faith even if God does not answer you quickly. God may delay in order to teach you many things, just as He taught Elisha that the power is from Him and not in material things in themselves. And if you do not quickly understand God's purpose, you will understand it if you continue in prayer, and your heart will be at rest.

2.14.0.en: When the sons of the prophets who dwelt at Jericho saw him coming toward them, they were certain that the spirit of Elijah rested on Elisha, so they came to meet him and bowed themselves before him, a bowing of respect and honor, acknowledging and being convinced that he had taken the place of Elijah.

2.15.0.en: After the sons of the prophets bowed to Elisha, because he had worked the miracle of dividing the river and they saw him alone without Elijah, their eyes were asking about Elijah. So Elisha told them what he had seen and how Elijah went up in the chariot of fire and the whirlwind to heaven until he disappeared from his sight. But because of these prophets' attachment to the great Elijah, and because of their spiritual weakness, they could not understand that Elijah had been taken to heaven and they would not see him again. They imagined that this chariot of fire could carry him from one place to another, so that it was merely a declaration of the greatness of their prophet Elijah, for whom a chariot comes from heaven to carry him to another place. They understood that this chariot and its horses were angels, that is, that the Spirit of God was the One who lifted him up to heaven, and they thought that the chariot had carried him to one of the mountains or valleys. So they asked Elisha, to whom they had submitted as their new leader, to allow them to search for Elijah, especially as their number was large, fifty men. Elisha refused, being confident that his master had gone up to heaven. The prophets thought that Elijah had been taken to another place because they were accustomed to his disappearing from them for periods, for he loved solitude and prayer all his life, and they did not understand that this was the end.

2.16.0.en: Although Elisha forbade the prophets to search for Elijah, they repeated their request many times, until Elisha was ashamed before them. This shows the gentleness of his feelings, for he is mighty by the power of God that supports him, but his feelings are tender and as a man he is ashamed at people's insistence on him. So he agreed to go and search for Elijah, although he was not convinced of what they were doing and was confident that Elijah had gone up to the heavens.

2.16.1.en: Another reason for his agreement was that they might not think he loved leadership and was hasty to lead the people and did not want Elijah to return, so that he might be the leader.

2.16.2.en: They searched for Elijah three days and did not find him, and this was a certain declaration that he had gone up to the heavens and had not gone to some other place on earth.

2.17.0.en: Elisha stayed at Jericho three days, until the sons of the prophets returned to him and told him that they had not found Elijah. He said to them, Did I not say unto you, Go not? That is, why did you doubt what I told you? This was a second divine declaration, after his dividing the river, that they ought to obey Elisha in everything, because the Spirit of God was in him. And Elisha here is a type of Christ, who is longsuffering toward the doubters and all who do not obey Him, just as He bore with the doubt of Thomas.

2.18.0.en: Naught: unfit to drink and harmful to health, and it may be poisonous.

2.18.2.en: Those responsible for the city of Jericho heard from the sons of the prophets what Elisha had done in dividing the Jordan River, and that he had become the prophet and leader of the people. So they seized the opportunity of his presence in their city for him to solve a basic problem from which they suffered, which was that although the position of their city was fine, at the foot of the mountain with the valley of the Jordan River in front of it, the main spring that watered the city had water that was unfit for drinking or farming. Perhaps they drank from small wells inside or outside the city, but farming was almost nonexistent for lack of sufficient water for farming.

2.19.0.en: Elisha cared about their problem and came forward to solve it for them, so that when they saw the miracle they might believe in God and turn away from the worship of idols. He asked for a new cruse, and this signifies the renewal of conduct and of life with God, so that He may bless us and work in us with power. Then he also asked for salt to be put in the cruse. Salt is not a substance for improving water but for spoiling it, for salty water does not become fit for drinking or farming; but this was to show that the power is from God and not from the substance. He used a substance to be visible to people's eyes and tangible, that they might be assured of the completion of the miracle, just as the Church uses materials in the performance of her seven sacraments. Salt signifies the believers who improve the earth by their pure conduct, as salt improves food so that its taste is good; therefore Christ said, Ye are the salt of the earth (Mt 5:13). Of course a little salt cannot improve a whole spring of water, but what is meant is the power of God, which works and uses a substance to reassure people's hearts.

2.20.0.en: Elisha took the dish and the salt and went out to the spring of water and cast the salt into it, and declared in faith that the water was healed, and that there was no longer in it any foreign substance that causes the death of man, or animal, or plant, that is, it became sweet and fit for drinking and farming. This water remained sweet until the days of Jeremiah, when this book was written, and it is thought that this spring still exists today and is called "the Sultan's Spring."

2.20.1.en: Do not be troubled by any problem that befalls you, but resort to God, intercede through the saints and seek the guidance of your spiritual fathers, confident that God will not leave you and will solve your problems, for He is able to do all things.

2.21.0.en: After Elisha worked his great miracle at Jericho, he went to Bethel to visit the school of the prophets and care for its people. Bethel was the seat of the worship of the calf that Jeroboam made, who was the first to divide the Jews into two kingdoms and made his people worship idols. We may recall that "Bethel" means "house of God," and it is the city and the place that Jacob set apart to the name of God after he saw Him in his dream there. Of course its inhabitants refused to hear the words of the prophets because of their unbelief in God, and even mocked them. So when the people of Bethel saw Elisha coming from afar, they stirred up their youths, who came out of the city in great numbers, perhaps two hundred or three hundred, and received Elisha with fierce mockery, taunting him that he was bald and repeating this more than once in derision of him. Perhaps by "go up" they meant, go up to heaven like your master Elijah, who you imagine went up to heaven, that is, they were mocking him because they did not believe that Elijah went up to heaven, nor in Elisha's dignity as a prophet. This is exceedingly strange, because they had certainly heard of his miracle in healing the water at Jericho and how all its people rejoiced in it.

2.22.0.en: The wilderness: desolate places not inhabited by people.

2.22.1.en: Elisha looked at the crowds of youths mocking him and was not troubled for his own sake, but was troubled by the city's insistence on rejecting God, showing it by mocking His prophet. He proclaimed God's wrath on the city by cursing those youths, so two she bears came out of the wilderness and fell upon the boys and killed forty and two boys of them. Because Elisha did not intend personal rage but the glory of God, God answered his curse on the children, and the two bears came out and killed a number of them, that perhaps the people of the city would fear God and leave the worship of idols and return in repentance.

2.22.2.en: God sometimes uses tenderness and love to draw His children to Himself, or wrath in severe afflictions, to draw them also to Himself, for He desires the salvation of all and uses various ways for the repentance of His children. I wish you would heed God's messages, whether His tenderness or His wrath, and return to Him in repentance and find the salvation of your soul.

2.23.0.en: Carmel: a range of mountains clothed with fruitful forests, near Jaffa, which is on the coast of the Mediterranean Sea, and Carmel overlooks the plain of Jezreel.

2.23.1.en: Samaria: the capital of the northern kingdom, which comprises the ten tribes, and it lies in a middle place between Galilee in the north and Judea in the south.

2.23.2.en: Elisha went to Carmel, where Elijah killed the prophets of Baal, and from there he went to Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom, and there he made his home (ch. 5:3, 9; ch. 6:32). King Jehoram and the war against Moab.
